payload.title: Same Whole, Same Unit
payload.objective: Explain why fractions must share one whole before their quantities are compared, how the denominator names the unit and the numerator counts units, how one positive integer preserves quantity, and how a common unit makes addition valid.
payload.introduction: When a fraction question feels mechanical, return to three questions: What is the whole? What unit does the denominator name? How many units does the numerator count? The rules for comparing fractions, forming equivalent fractions, and adding fractions follow from those answers.
payload.concept: A fraction describes selected equal parts of one whole. Begin by naming that whole. The denominator names the unit, and the numerator counts how many such units are selected. Fractions must refer to the same whole before their quantities can be compared; if the wholes differ, describe their sizes instead of treating the fractions alone as a sufficient comparison. Equivalent fractions represent the same quantity only when both numerator and denominator are multiplied by the same positive integer; this changes the partition without changing the quantity, as in 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. To add 1/2 and 1/3 of the same whole, use sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Adding the denominators gives the wrong unit. For positive addends, the sum should be greater than either addend; here it is also less than one whole. A correct numerical answer with an unexplained unit still needs a reasoning check.
notes: Identify the whole before comparing fractions.
Denominator: the unit; numerator: how many units.
Same whole is required for comparison.
Equivalent fractions: same positive integer on top and bottom.
Add only after choosing a common unit.

example.scenario: Two fractions describe parts of one identical whole: 1/2 and 1/3. The units are halves and thirds, so add after converting to a common unit.
steps: Name the whole: both fractions refer to the same whole.
Name the units: halves and thirds are different units.
Choose sixths: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6.
Add counts of sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
Check that 5/6 is greater than either addend and less than one whole.
board: Adding denominators gives the wrong unit
example.conclusion: The sum is 5/6 of the same whole. The common unit makes the counts addable; the numerical result still needs a reasoning check about the unit and whole.

misconception.correction: Only multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer preserves quantity; changing only one part does not. The condition applies to both parts of the fraction, and the integer must be positive.

lesson.transfer: When a new task gives two wholes, do not compare or add the fractions until you confirm the wholes are the same. Name each unit, choose a common partition when needed, and check the result against the positive-addend expectation. If the wholes differ, describe their sizes instead of treating the fractions alone as sufficient.
lesson.summary: Fractions are selected equal parts of the same whole. The denominator names the unit; the numerator counts selected units. Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same positive integer preserves quantity. With the same whole, 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
takeaways: Fractions need the same whole before comparison.
Denominator names the unit; numerator counts units.
Use the same positive multiplier for equivalence.

citations.quote: A fraction describes selected equal parts of the same whole.
The denominator names the unit and the numerator counts how many such units are selected.
multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer changes the partition without changing the quantity
To add 1/2 and 1/3 of the same whole, use sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
A counterexample guards the same-whole condition: half of a small cake need not equal half of a large cake.

questions.prompt: Before comparing two fraction quantities, what condition does the source require?
options: They must refer to the same whole.
They must have the same numerator.
They must have different denominators.
They must each be less than one.
questions.explanation: The source states that fractions must refer to the same whole before their quantities can be compared.
hints: Look for the condition tied to comparing quantities.
The condition concerns the whole, not the numerator.

questions.prompt: In the fraction 3/6, what does the denominator 6 name?
options: The number of selected parts
The size of the original whole
The unit being counted
The number of wholes
questions.explanation: The denominator names the unit, while the numerator counts how many selected units there are.
hints: Separate the naming role from the counting role.
The numerator counts selected parts.

questions.prompt: Which expression correctly adds 1/2 and 1/3 of the same whole by using sixths?
questions.explanation: Using sixths gives 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so the sum is 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
hints: Rewrite each fraction with the same unit first.
Do not add the denominators.

questions.prompt: Which operation uses the positive-integer equivalence rule described in the source?
options: Add the same number to numerator and denominator.
Multiply numerator and denominator by different positive integers.
Multiply only the denominator by a positive integer.
Multiply both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer.
questions.explanation: Multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same positive integer changes the partition without changing the quantity.
hints: Look for the operation applied to both parts.
The multiplier must be positive and the same.

issues.detail: The single assigned chunk also requires that a drawn model label the whole and show equal-sized parts, and that a proposed answer be checked by converting it back into the original quantities. The draft omits both source requirements without an explicit omission reason, so coverage of the assigned chunk is incomplete.
